title: FGF 13 functions as a regulator of the ERK/aerobic glycolysis axis in the inflammatory state during septic lung injury

paper_content.abstract: Fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13) belongs to the FGF homologous factor subfamily, members of which lack signal peptides. In this study, we demonstrate that FGF13 is significantly downregulated in endothelial cells and macrophages in the lungs of septic patients and septic mice. However, the role of FGF13 in sepsis and the underlying mechanism are largely unknown. By using mice with conditional Fgf13 knockout and FGF13 overexpression, we find that FGF13 accelerates septic lung injury by promoting inflammatory activation of endothelial cells and macrophages. Specifically, FGF13 functions as a scaffold protein in TAK1/MEK/ERK signaling to promote hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)−1α-regulated aerobic glycolysis in the inflammatory state. Meanwhile, the protective effect of conditional Fgf13 knockout is abolished in HIF-1α-overexpressing mice. In addition, SCH772984 (a selective antagonist of ERK signaling) abolishes the aggravation of inflammation in lungs induced by FGF13 overexpression. Our findings demonstrate that FGF13 promotes inflammatory activation upon septic lung injury through the ERK/aerobic glycolysis axis, thereby accelerating the progression of septic lung injury.
paper_content.introduction:
As a critical public health emergency, sepsis has had an average annual rate of about 50 million cases globally since 2017, with a mortality rate of approximately 20%, resulting in a financial burden of around $20 billion in the United States alone1. Despite decades of clinical research on sepsis, treatment strategies for this disease remain limited to antibiotics, steroids, supplements, and organ support. These broad-spectrum interventions not only exhibit limited effectiveness but also frequently lead to various side effects, which impact patient prognosis2. Therefore, gaining a deeper understanding of the pathogenesis of sepsis and developing more targeted and safer therapeutic strategies based on this enhanced understanding has significant clinical implications.

During the progression of sepsis, the direct damage caused by pathogens and the excessive inflammatory response induce multi-organ damage, potentially culminating in organ failure and mortality. Among these complications, septic lung injury is the most prevalent and serious manifestation3,4. When pathogen-associated molecular patterns (e.g., lipopolysaccharide (LPS), mitochondrial DNA, and lipoteichoic acid) produced by pathogens destroy the barrier integrity of lung epithelial and endothelial cells or even kill them, they lead to the inflammatory activation of these cells, which results in recruitment of immune cells (e.g., neutrophils and monocytes (macrophages)) into the lung microenvironment to fight pathogens5–7. Although immune cells clear pathogens and cell debris from the lungs, they also lead to “an inflammatory storm” (e.g., interleukin (IL)−1β, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α) and production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These inflammatory cytokines and ROS aggravate the injury of lung epithelial and endothelial cells, further exacerbate the infiltration of immune cells, impair gas exchange, and ultimately lead to respiratory failure8,9. In this process, endothelial cells serve as “initiators” in the development of lung inflammation, while macrophages function as “amplifiers” of inflammatory injury, and both play crucial roles as mediators of septic lung injury. Consequently, inhibition of inflammatory cell infiltration resulting from inflammatory activation of endothelial cells or suppression of the inflammatory storm induced by macrophages can effectively mitigate septic lung injury and reduce the mortality rate of sepsis10.

Fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13) belongs to the FGF homologous factor subfamily, which differs from other FGF subfamilies because its members all lack signal peptides and cannot be secreted conventionally11. FGF13 has been extensively studied in the nervous system, and our recent research revealed that it disrupts endothelial cell homeostasis by modulating mitophagy through Parkin, exacerbating diabetic nephropathy12. Additionally, another study of ours demonstrated that FGF12 (homologous to FGF13) regulates macrophage polarization to promote liver fibrosis13. However, it remains unknown whether FGF13 participates in the pathological progression of septic lung injury, which is mainly mediated by endothelial cells and macrophages.

Here, we found that FGF13 was downregulated in endothelial cells and macrophages in the lungs of septic mice and septic patients. FGF13 promoted inflammatory activation of both endothelial cells and macrophages upon LPS stimulation in vitro.

Here, we show, by using two mouse models (injection of LPS (endotoxic shock) and cecal ligation and puncture (CLP)), we find that septic lung injury is alleviated in mice with endothelial cell-specific (Fgf13△Endo) and myeloid cell-specific (Fgf13△mye) Fgf13 knockout, but is aggravated in mice with endothelial cell-specific (CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13) and myeloid cell-specific (LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13) FGF13 overexpression. To further investigate the mechanisms of FGF13 in sepsis, we performed co-immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry. This demonstrates that FGF13 functions as a scaffold protein in the TAK1/MEK/ERK axis to regulate hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)−1α-induced aerobic glycolysis, which promotes inflammatory activation of endothelial cells and macrophages, ultimately contributing to septic lung injury.
paper_content.results:
FGF13 is downregulated in endothelial cells and macrophages in septic lungs

FGFs are critical regulators of lung development and microenvironment homeostasis14. Prior studies indicate that specific FGFs (e.g., FGF1, FGF2, FGF9, and FGF10) modulate pulmonary immune responses and repair processes15–18. During sepsis, perturbation of homeostasis in the lung microenvironment substantially alters FGF expression. To systematically profile these changes, we performed RNA sequencing of lung tissues from healthy and LPS-treated mice, and validated the findings via qRT-PCR using human samples (non-septic patients vs. septic patients). FGF2 was consistently upregulated in both species during sepsis, while FGF1, FGF10, FGF13, FGF14, and FGF18 were downregulated (Fig. 1A–C). While the roles of most of these FGFs (except FGF13/FGF14) have been characterized16,19–21, our recent discovery of the regulatory function of FGF13 in endothelial homeostasis prompted us to investigate its specific role in septic lung injury and the underlying mechanisms.

Consistent with its mRNA level, the protein level of FGF13 was decreased in lungs of septic mice and septic patients (Fig. 1D, E). Additionally, the protein level of FGF13 in lungs of moribund mice in LPS injection model was negatively correlated with survival time (Fig. 1F). After confirming through H&E staining that CLP induced significant pulmonary pathological changes (with evident inflammatory cell infiltration) (Fig. 1G), to further clarify the main cell types that express FGF13 in the lungs, we performed immunofluorescence analysis of FGF13 and various cell markers (AQP5, SPC, CD34, and F4/80) in mice. Endothelial cells were the major cell type that expressed FGF13, followed by macrophages. Expression of FGF13 was relatively low in both types of epithelial cells. Upon CLP operation, the number of FGF13-positive endothelial cells and macrophages greatly decreased in lungs of mice (Fig. 1H–L). Consistently, the alterations in the protein level of FGF13 and colocalization of FGF13 with different cell markers were similar in LPS-treated mice (Fig. S1A–G). Consistent with the findings in septic mice, colocalization of FGF13 with endothelial cells and macrophages was decreased in septic patients (Fig. 1M–O). Furthermore, we confirmed these observations in vitro. After LPS treatment, the protein level of FGF13 was decreased in human pulmonary microvascular endothelial cells (HPMECs) and THP-1 cells (Fig. S1H, I). These results suggest that expression of FGF13 in endothelial cells and macrophages is downregulated in the inflammatory state, which might modulate the progression of septic lung injury.

FGF13 promotes inflammatory activation of endothelial cells to aggravate immune cell infiltration upon septic lung injury

To explore the role of FGF13 in septic lung injury, we used Ad-shFgf13/Ad-Fgf13 to knockdown or overexpress FGF13 in HPMECs (Fig. S2A, B). In an endothelial cell inflammatory activation model, the LPS-induced increases of the protein levels of VCAM-1 and ICAM-1, as well as the mRNA levels of Ccl2, Vcam-1, and Icam-1 were attenuated in Fgf13-knockdown HPMECs but enhanced in Fgf13-overexpressing HPMECs (Fig. S2C–F). Fgf13 knockdown reduced monocyte adhesion to LPS-stimulated HPMECs (Fig. S2G–J), whereas LPS induced greater monocyte adhesion to Fgf13-overexpressing HPMECs (Fig. S2K–N). These results indicate that FGF13 promotes LPS-induced inflammatory activation of endothelial cells.

To further validate these findings in vivo, we generated endothelial cell-specific Fgf13 knockout (Fgf13△Endo) mice by crossbreeding transgenic mice, as well as endothelial cell-specific FGF13 overexpression (CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13) mice by injecting AAV-lung-DIO-Fgf13 (Fig. S3A–C). In both models (CLP and injection of LPS), Fgf13△Endo mice had a higher survival rate than CDH5-Cre controls, while CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice had a lower survival rate (Fig. 2A, S4A). Assessment of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) protein concentrations/cell counts, lung wet-to-dry weight ratios, and lung morphology revealed that sepsis-induced lung edema and hemorrhage were significantly alleviated in Fgf13△Endo mice but exacerbated in CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Figs. 2B–F, S4B–F). Consistent with the in vitro data, lung tissue expression of endothelial cell inflammatory activation markers (iNOS, ICAM-1, and VCAM-1) was lower in Fgf13△Endo and higher in CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice than in CDH5-Cre controls in both models (Figs. 2G, H, S4G, H). Reflecting this endothelial cell inflammatory activation, hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining and myeloperoxidase (MPO)/F4/80 immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that inflammatory cell infiltration (neutrophils and macrophages) was significantly reduced in lungs of septic Fgf13△Endo mice but increased in those of septic CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Figs. 2I–M, S4I–M). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that FGF13 promotes endothelial cell inflammatory activation during sepsis, thereby exacerbating inflammatory cell infiltration and aggravating septic lung injury.

FGF13 promotes inflammatory activation of macrophages to amplify inflammation upon septic lung injury

Considering that FGF13 also exhibited expression changes in macrophages, which play a pivotal role in septic lung injury, we were intrigued by the possibility that it influences inflammatory activation of these cells. Building upon the methodologies employed in endothelial cells, we used Ad-shFgf13/Ad-Fgf13 to knock down or overexpress FGF13 in THP-1 cells (Fig. S5A, B). Upon LPS stimulation, the increase of the protein level of iNOS and the increase of the mRNA levels of Il-1β, Il-6, and Tnf-α were relieved in Fgf13-knockdown THP-1 cells and aggravated in Fgf13-overexpressing THP-1 cells (Fig. S5C–F). Compared with the culture medium of Ad-vector-transfected THP-1 cells, that of Fgf13-knockdown THP-1 cells induced less apoptosis and barrier loss in HPMECs, while that of Fgf13-overexpressing THP-1 cells induced more (Fig. S5G–N). These results indicate that FGF13 promotes LPS-induced inflammatory activation of macrophages.

To further validate these findings in vivo, we generated macrophage-specific Fgf13 knockout (Fgf13△mye) mice by crossbreeding transgenic mice as well as macrophage-specific FGF13 overexpression (LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13) mice by injecting AAV-lung-DIO-Fgf13 (Figure S6A–C). Consistent with the results in endothelial cells, Fgf13△mye mice had a higher survival rate than CDH5-Cre mice in both models, while LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice had a lower survival rate (Fig. 3A, S7A). BALF analysis and lung morphology observation revealed that sepsis-induced lung edema, hemorrhage, and inflammatory cell infiltration were significantly alleviated in Fgf13△mye mice, but aggravated in LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Figs. 3B–G, S7B–G). In line with the in vitro results, inflammatory activation of macrophages was restrained in lungs of Fgf13△mye mice in both models, but aggravated in lungs of LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Figs. 3H, I, S7H, I). Furthermore, compared with LyzM-Cre mice during sepsis, Fgf13△mye mice displayed lower serum levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α, while the opposite was true in LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Figs. 3J, S7J). Likewise, sepsis-induced cell apoptosis and barrier loss in lungs were mitigated in Fgf13△mye mice, but aggravated in LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Figs. 3K–N, S7K–N). Collectively, these findings suggest that FGF13 accelerates inflammatory activation of macrophages during sepsis, leading to the production of large amounts of inflammatory cytokines and exacerbation of septic lung injury.

FGF13 promotes aerobic glycolysis in the inflammatory state

Beyond its established functions in the nervous system, FGF13 plays significant roles in colorectal cancer, breast cancer, and several other malignancies22–24. Cancer cells undergo metabolic reprogramming from oxidative phosphorylation to aerobic glycolysis in order to fuel their rapid proliferation, migration, and invasion. This metabolic shift is strikingly similar to that observed in endothelial cells and macrophages during inflammatory activation25,26. Notably, elevated lactate levels resulting from enhanced aerobic glycolysis correlate strongly with mortality rates in septic patients27. Recent investigations of glucose homeostasis revealed an inverse relationship between FGF13 expression and the peripheral blood glucose concentration28. Considering the critical role of aerobic glycolysis in mediating pro-inflammatory responses of both endothelial and immune cells, we postulated that FGF13 may regulate inflammation progression by modulating glucose metabolism pathways.

As expected, in both models, the levels of lactate were lower in the peripheral blood of Fgf13△Endo and Fgf13△mye mice than in the peripheral blood of corresponding control mice, whereas the opposite was true in CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 and LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice (Fig. S8A–D). Consistent with the findings of the in vivo studies, the results of the Seahorse XF glycolysis stress test suggested that the aerobic glycolysis capacity of pro-inflammatory HPMECs and THP-1 cells was significantly reduced by knockdown of FGF13, but amplified by overexpression of FGF13 (Fig. 4A–D). Both 2-NBDG fluorescence staining and glucose uptake experiments revealed that glucose uptake and lactate production in pro-inflammatory HPMECs and THP-1 cells were notably disrupted by knockdown of FGF13 (Fig. 4E–L), but enhanced by overexpression of FGF13 (Fig. 4M–T). Subsequent investigations revealed that PFK15 (a glycolysis inhibitor29) mitigated inflammatory activation of Fgf13-overexpressing HPMECs, resulting in decreased monocyte adhesion (Fig. S8E–H). Moreover, PFK15 reduced the elevated levels of iNOS protein and secretion of IL-6 and TNF-α in Fgf13-overexpressing THP-1 cells (Figure S8I, J). Overall, these findings underscore the role of FGF13 in promoting aerobic glycolysis in endothelial cells and macrophages under inflammatory conditions, contributing to the amplification of their inflammatory response.

FGF13 regulates aerobic glycolysis via ERK/HIF-1α signaling

During inflammatory responses, aerobic glycolysis is sophisticatedly regulated by multiple signaling cascades, including the AMPK-mTOR, ERK/HIF-1α, and NF-κB pathways25. To elucidate the precise molecular mechanism by which FGF13 modulates inflammatory aerobic glycolysis, we performed unbiased proteomic analysis via mass spectrometry of lysates of FGF13-overexpressing HEK293 cells (Fig. 5A). This comprehensive screening identified MAPK1 (ERK2) as a high-confidence interaction partner of FGF13 (Fig. 5B). Based on this protein–protein interaction, we hypothesized that FGF13 regulates inflammation-induced aerobic glycolysis primarily through the ERK/HIF-1α signaling axis, which is a well-established pathway in metabolic reprogramming during inflammatory activation.

As expected, knockdown of FGF13 significantly reduced the elevated phosphorylation levels of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 as well as the protein level of HIF-1α in LPS-treated HPMECs and THP-1 cells, while overexpression of FGF13 further upregulated the phosphorylation levels of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 as well as the protein level of HIF-1α (Fig. 5C–F). When cells were pretreated with SCH772984 (a specific ERK1/2 inhibitor)30, the enhanced aerobic glycolysis capacity of Fgf13-overexpressing HPMECs was abolished, and the increased glucose uptake and lactate production were also abrogated (Figs. 5G, S9A–E). Consistently, SCH772984 counteracted the increased monocyte adhesion to LPS-treated Fgf13-overexpressing HPMECs (Fig. S9F–I). Similarly, pretreatment with SCH772984 abolished the enhanced aerobic glycolysis capacity of Fgf13-overexpressing THP-1 cells, leading to decreased glucose uptake and lactate production in LPS-treated THP-1 cells (Figs. 5H, S9J–N). Moreover, SCH772984 reduced the elevated levels of iNOS protein and secretion of IL-6 and TNF-α in Fgf13-overexpressing THP-1 cells (Fig. S9O, P). Collectively, these results indicate that the role of FGF13 in promoting aerobic glycolysis to exacerbate inflammatory activation of endothelial cells and macrophages depends on ERK/HIF-1α signaling.

The protective effect of FGF13 knockout on septic lung injury is abolished in HIF-1α-overexpressing mice

To further substantiate our findings in vivo, we engineered mice with endothelial cell-specific and macrophage-specific HIF-1α overexpression by administering AAV-lung-DIO-hif1a. Following confirmation of successful HIF-1α overexpression in endothelial cells, we observed that HIF-1α overexpression reversed the protective effects seen in Fgf13△Endo mice in both models, including reduced peripheral blood lactate levels and improved survival rates (Fig. S10A–E). Comprehensive assessment of lung pathology, including wet-to-dry weight ratios, morphological observation, H&E staining, and immunofluorescence detection of MPO/F4/80 demonstrated that the attenuated lung edema, hemorrhage, and inflammatory cell infiltration (neutrophils and macrophages) in Fgf13△Endo mice in both models were completely negated by AAV-lung-DIO-hif1a administration (Figs. 6A–H, S10F–M). Similarly, after injection of AAV-lung-DIO-hif1a, the peripheral blood lactate levels and survival rate of Fgf13△mye mice did not significantly differ from those of LyzM-Cre mice in both models (Fig. S11A–E). Following LPS challenge or the CLP procedure, HIF-1α overexpression counteracted both the suppression of the inflammatory activation of pulmonary macrophages and the downregulation of serum pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α) observed in Fgf13△mye mice (Figs. 6I, J, S11F-I). Likewise, measurement of lung wet-to-dry weight ratios, observation of lung morphology, H&E staining, and fluorescence staining of VE-cadherin in lungs of each group revealed that the reductions of hemorrhage, inflammatory cell infiltration, and barrier loss in Fgf13△mye mice were abolished by AAV-lung-DIO-hif1a in both models (Figs. 6K–P, S11J–O). These findings suggest that FGF13 worsens septic lung injury by promoting HIF-1α-induced aerobic glycolysis in endothelial cells and macrophages.

FGF13 acts as a scaffold protein in TAK1/MEK/ERK signaling

Figure S12A shows the activation process of the ERK signaling pathway upon LPS stimulation. Knockdown of Fgf13 in HPMECs and THP-1 cells did not affect phosphorylation of TAK1 at Thr184/Thr187 (which is critical for ERK signaling activation31) (Fig. S12B, C), indicating that FGF13 does not affect the upstream signaling of TAK1. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) revealed that FGF13 can interact with ERK2; therefore, we speculated that FGF13 is involved in activation of the TAK1-MEK-ERK signaling axis through protein binding. Co-immunoprecipitation experiments showed that FGF13 interacted with TAK1, MEK1/2, and ERK1/2 in HPMECs and THP-1 cells, and these interactions were enhanced upon LPS stimulation (Figs. 7A, B, S13A–D). Similarly, immunofluorescence experiments demonstrated the clear colocalization of FGF13 with TAK1, MEK1/2, and ERK1/2 in these cells (Fig. 7C, D). To further validate our hypothesis, we transfected HEK293 cells with plasmids encoding Flag-FGF13, HA-TAK1, HA-MEK1, HA-MEK2, HA-ERK1, and HA-ERK2. As expected, exogenous FGF13 interacted with exogenous TAK1, MEK1, MEK2, ERK1, and ERK2 in HEK293 cells (Fig. 7E–I). Additionally, GST pull-down assays indicated that FGF13 interacted directly with TAK1, MEK1, MEK2, ERK1, and ERK2 (Fig. 7J). Based on these findings, we speculated that FGF13 acts as a scaffold protein in the TAK1-MEK-ERK axis. In LPS-treated HPMECs and THP-1 cells, the interaction between MEK1 and TAK1, as well as ERK1/2, was reduced by knockdown of Fgf13, but enhanced by overexpression of Fgf13 (Fig. 7K–N). Thus, FGF13 promotes activation of the TAK1-MEK-ERK axis by functioning as a scaffold protein to strengthen the interactions between components.

Despite our finding that FGF13 is a critical scaffold protein that facilitates activation of the TAK1-MEK-ERK signaling axis, we observed a paradoxical decrease in FGF13 protein expression in both HPMECs and THP-1 cells under inflammatory conditions. This intriguing contradiction prompted further mechanistic investigation. Previous studies reported p53-mediated transcriptional repression of miR-504 and its host gene Fgf13, while other evidence indicates that septic conditions activate p53 signaling pathways, consequently accelerating apoptosis and DNA damage during disease progression32,33. Integrating these molecular insights, we postulated that inflammatory downregulation of FGF13 might occur through p53-dependent mechanisms. To test this hypothesis, we employed RNA interference strategies targeting p53 in both HPMECs and THP-1 cells. Remarkably, p53 knockdown abolished the LPS-induced downregulation of FGF13 protein, providing compelling evidence that p53 is the critical mediator of inflammatory FGF13 downregulation in both endothelial cells and macrophages (Figure S14A–D). This regulatory mechanism reveals an important homeostatic circuit in which inflammatory stimuli trigger p53-dependent suppression of an otherwise pro-inflammatory signaling scaffold molecule.

SCH772984 mitigates the exacerbation of septic lung injury by FGF13

To further confirm that the role of FGF13 in exacerbating septic lung injury relies on ERK signaling, we administered the ERK signaling antagonist SCH772984 to CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 and LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice in order to inhibit ERK activation following LPS challenge or the CLP procedure (Figs. S15A, B, S16A, B). In CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice, SCH772984 robustly counteracted the pathological elevation of peripheral blood lactate levels and substantially ameliorated the aggravated pulmonary edema and hemorrhage in both models (Figs. 8A–C, S15C–G). Histopathological analysis through H&E staining and fluorescence staining of MPO/F4/80 revealed that ERK inhibition substantially diminished the enhanced neutrophil and macrophage infiltration in lungs of CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice following LPS challenge or the CLP procedure (Figs. 8D–H, S15H–L).

In parallel experiments with LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice, SCH772984 similarly attenuated the pathological elevation of peripheral blood lactate levels under septic conditions (Fig. S16C, D). Notably, ERK inhibition profoundly suppressed both the augmented pulmonary accumulation of pro-inflammatory macrophages and the elevated systemic levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α) in LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice in both sepsis models (Figs. 8I, J, S16E- H). Consequently, SCH772984 significantly mitigated the enhanced pulmonary pathologies (edema, hemorrhage, inflammatory cell infiltration, and endothelial barrier disruption) in LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice following LPS challenge or the CLP procedure (Fig. 8K–P, S16I–N). Collectively, these pharmacological intervention studies provide compelling evidence that FGF13 amplifies septic lung injury primarily by augmenting ERK signaling pathways in both endothelial cells and macrophages.
paper_content.methods:
Cell culture
HPMECs were obtained from ScienCell Research Laboratories (3000) and cultured according to the instructions. THP1 cells (CL-0233) and HEK293T cells (CL-0005) were purchased from Procell. To knockdown or overexpress FGF13 in HPMECs and THP1 cells, Ad-shFgf13 or Ad-Fgf13 was transfected to HPMECs and THP1 cells. After 48 h, the culture medium was removed, and the cells were used in the following experiments. For experimental purposes, Ad-vector-transfected HPMECs or THP1 cells were used as control group in subsequent experiments. To induce THP-1 cells into macrophages, PMA (200 ng/ml; Selleck, S7791) was used to treat THP-1 cells for 48 hours before adenovirus transfection. Primary endothelial cells in lungs and primary macrophages in lungs were isolated as previously51,52.
LPS (1 μg/ml; Sigma Aldrich, L6386) was used to stimulate HPMECs and THP1 cells. In signaling pathway analysis, each antagonist: PFK15 (30 μM; Selleck, S7289), SCH772984 (10 μM; Selleck, S7101) was pretreated for 12 h before LPS administration.

Detection of 2-NBDG fluorescence
After 12 hours of LPS stimulation, the culture medium from HPMECs or THP-1 cells was washed twice with PBS. Then added complete culture medium containing 2-NBDG (20 μM; GLPBIO, GC10289). After incubating at 37 °C for 30 minutes, the culture medium was again washed twice with PBS, and then the complete culture medium was added. Then, the phenomenon of 2-NBDG in each group was analyzed in 30 minutes (ZEISS LSM 980 with Airyscan2 Confocal microscope (ZEISS, Germany)).

ELISA analysis of biochemical parameters
Before measuring the biochemical parameters, peripheral blood was collected, allowed to settle overnight, and centrifuged (3000 × g, 10 min, 4 °C). The supernatant was used to measure the levels of inflammatory cytokines. Mouse-interleukin-1β (Proteintech, cat. no. KE10003), mouse-tumor necrosis factor-α (Proteintech, cat. no. KE10002), mouse-interleukin-6 (Proteintech, cat. no. KE10007), and Lactate (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, A019-2-1) were analyzed using a double antibody sandwich method according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Ethics statement
All human participants' research in this study was conducted in accordance with the principles of “World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki: ethical principles for medical research involving human participants”. Before collecting samples from non-septic patients (patients requiring surgical removal of lung nodules) and septic patients (patients who developed sepsis due to lung nodule-related infections and requiring surgical intervention), we provided informed consent forms (Supplementary materials: Informed consent form) to both categories of patients, and selected lung tissue distant from the nodule regions from the resected lung specimens for subsequent research. The biochemical indicators and information for each group of patients are included in Table S1: Information of patients. Patient data and pathological evaluations were approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University (Approval ID: KY2023-197-01). All animals in our study received humane care according to the criteria outlined in the “Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals.” Animal protocols were approved by the Ethics Committee of Wenzhou Medical University.

Extracellular metabolic flux analysis
Extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) of HPMECs or THP-1 cells was analyzed with an XF96 Extracellular Flux Analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience, North Billerica, MA, USA) as described previously53. Briefly, HPMECs or THP-1 cells were plated on Seahorse XF96 polystyrene tissue culture plates (Seahorse Bioscience) and incubated at 37 °C overnight. The next day, after 1 ug/ml LPS treatment for 12 hours, the medium was changed to XF base Medium (Seahorse Bioscience) supplemented with 2 mM glutamine, and then the plate was incubated for 1 h in a non-CO2 incubator at 37 °C. The ECAR assay was performed on the XF96 extracellular flux analyzer (Seahorse Bioscience), and the ECAR values were normalized using protein concentration. Inhibitors and activators used in these tests at the following concentrations: glucose (10 mM), oligomycin (2 μM), 2DG (50 mM).

Glucose Influx and Lactate Efflux Kinetics
HPMECs or THP-1 cells were plated in a 6-well plate. On the day of treatment, culture medium was refreshed, and cells were then stimulated with LPS. One milliliter of medium in each experimental condition was collected immediately after medium change and stimulus addition (time = 0 h), and after 12 h of incubation (time = 12 h). Glucose and lactate content in the medium were measured using glucose and L-lactate assay kits, respectively, according to the manufacturer’s protocols (Cayman, Ann Arbor, MI).

GST-Pull-down assay
HA-TAK1, HA-MEK1, HA-MEK2, HA-ERK1, and HA-ERK2 plasmids were transfected into HEK293 cells, respectively, and cells were lysed with IP lysates. HA-TAK1, HA-MEK1, HA-MEK2, HA-ERK1, and HA-ERK2 were purified by the kit (Beyotime, P9808). GST and GST-FGF13 were transfected into DH5α cells and were purified by GST beads (Beyotime, P2138) at 4 °C. The purified proteins (GST and GST-FGF13) were incubated with purified HA-TAK1, HA-MEK1, HA-MEK2, HA-ERK1, and HA-ERK2 proteins overnight at 4 °C. Then, the beads were washed 3 times with IP lysates. The complexes were boiled with 2× SDS loading buffer at 95 °C for 10 min, followed by western blotting analyses.

Histological analysis of lungs section
Lungs from mice in each group were divided into 5 μm sections. Histological analysis of tissue sections was performed by H&E staining with a Hematoxylin-Eosin Kit (Solarbio, cat. no. G1120). After sealing with neutral resin, images of the stained sections were captured under a microscope (Motic, PA53BIO).

Immunoblotting analysis
After measuring the protein concentration using the BCA method, 30 μg protein for per sample was resolved by SDS-PAGE in Tris-glycine gels and transferred to a PVDF membrane. The membrane was blocked with 5% non-fat milk (2 h, room temperature), washed three times in 1× TBST (5 min each time), and incubated (overnight at 4 °C or for 3 h at 37 °C) with primary antibodies. This was followed by incubation with HRP-goat-anti-mouse (Abcam, cat. no. ab205719) or HRP-goat-anti-rabbit (Abcam, cat. no. ab205718) secondary antibodies (2 h, room temperature). Prior to visualization with a Chemiluminescent HRP Substrate (Millipore, cat. no. WBKLS0500), the membranes were washed in 1× TBST (three times, 5 min each). After visualization, the proteins in the membranes were analyzed (ImageQuant 800, Amersham, Cytiva) and quantified (ImageQuant 5.2 software, Molecular Dynamics, Sunnyvale, CA). Primary antibodies were specific for: FGF13 (Thermofisher, MA5-27705), ICAM-1 (Affinity Biosciences, AF6088), VCAM-1 (HUABIO, ET1601-18), iNOS (Cell Signaling Technology, 13120), Bcl-2 (Cell Signaling Technology, 3498), Bax (Cell Signaling Technology, 14796), cleaved-caspase 3 (Cell Signaling Technology, 9664), HIF-1α (Affinity Biosciences, BF8002), phospho-MEK1/2 (HUABIO, ET1609-50), MEK1/2 (HUABIO, ET1602-3), phospho-ERK1/2 (Cell Signaling Technology, 4370), ERK1/2 (Cell Signaling Technology, 4695), Flag (HUABIO, HA601080), HA (Cell Signaling Technology, 3724), GST (Cell Signaling Technology, 2622), phospho-TAK1 (Affinity Biosciences, AF4379), p53 (Cell Signaling Technology, 2524), and TAK1 (Affinity Biosciences, AF7616). And the expression of β-actin (Cell Signaling Technology, 3700) was used as a loading control. The detailed information on antibodies is provided in Table S2. Information on Antibody.

Immunoprecipitation
500 μg protein of HPMECs or THP1 cells was incubated with primary antibody (overnight, 4 °C). Add immobilized antibody beads (Millipore, LSKMAGAG10) to cell lysates for 4 h on the next day. Washed beads with TBS for 3 times, and eluted (glycine-HCl (0.1 M, pH 3.5)), then subjected to immunoblotting analysis. Immobilized antibody included: Flag (HUABIO, HA601080), HA (Cell Signaling Technology, 3724), TAK1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-7967), MEK1/2 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-81504), ERK1/2 (Cell Signaling Technology, 4695), and MEK1 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-6250). The detailed information on antibodies is provided in Table S2. Information on Antibody.

Immunofluorescence staining
Lung sections (5 μm) were heated at 96 °C for 5 min for antigen retrieval, followed by permeabilization with 0.5 % Triton X-100 (30 min, room temperature). The sections were washed three times in 1× PBST (5 min each time), blocked with 5 % BSA (30 min, room temperature), and incubated overnight at 4 °C with primary antibodies. The next day, lung sections were washed three times with 1× PBST (5 min each), followed by incubation with a secondary antibody (2 h, room temperature). Finally, the sections were washed three times with 1× PBST (5 min each) and nuclei stained with DAPI (30 min, room temperature). The primary antibodies were specific for AQP5 (Proteintech, 20334-1-AP), SPC-Ⅱ (Proteintech, 10774-1-AP), CD34 (HUABIO, ET1606-11), MPO (Abcam, ab208670), F4/80 (Cell Signaling Technology, 30325), CD86 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-28347) and VE-cadherin (Abcam, ab33168). After washing 3 times with PBS, lung sections were incubated with secondary antibody (2 h, room temperature). The secondary antibodies included: Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG H&L (Abcam, ab150077), Goat Anti-Mouse IgG H&L (Abcam, ab150113), Goat Anti-Rabbit IgG H&L (Abcam, ab150083) and Goat Anti-Mouse IgG H&L (Abcam, ab150115). DAPI was used to stain the nucleus.
In immunofluorescence staining of cells, HPMECs or THP1 cells in each group were fixed (4 % formaldehyde, 15 min, room temperature), permeabilized (0.5 % Triton X-100, 30 min, room temperature), blocked (5 % BSA, 30 min, room temperature), and incubated with primary antibodies (overnight, 4 °C). The primary antibodies included: VE-cadherin (Abcam, ab33168), FGF13 (Thermofisher, MA5-27705), TAK1 (HUABIO, ER1802-90), MEK1/2 (HUABIO, ET1602-3) and ERK1/2 (Cell Signaling Technology, 4695). After washing 3 times with PBS, HPMECs or THP1 cells were incubated with secondary antibody (2 h, room temperature). The secondary antibodies used in immunofluorescence staining of HPMECs or THP1 cells were consistent with immunofluorescence staining of lung sections. DAPI was used to stain the nucleus. The phenomenon in lung sections and cell sections of each group was analyzed (ZEISS LSM 980 with Airyscan2 Confocal microscope (ZEISS, Germany)). The detailed information on antibodies is provided in Table S2. Information on Antibody.

Measurement of cell number in BALF
BALF was collected as described previously54. The collected BALF was centrifuged at 2000 g to collect cells for further counting. And the supernatant was used to determine total protein concentration by Pierce BCA Protein Assay Reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23228).

Mice cohorts and treatment
C57BL/6 male mice in our study were purchased from the Model Animal Research Center of Nanjing University. To generate CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice and CDH5-CreDIO-hif1α mice, we injected AAV-lung-CMV-DIO-Fgf13-P2A-EGFP-tWPA (5 × 1012 vg/ml, OBIO technology (Shanghai), reference sequence of Fgf13: NM_010200.3) or AAV-lung-CMV-DIO-hif-1α-P2A-EGFP-tWPA (5 × 1012 vg/ml, OBIO technology (Shanghai), reference sequence of hif1α: NM_010431.2) intravenously to four-week-old CDH5-Cre mice. Steadily overexpressed for three weeks, CDH5-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice and CDH5-CreDIO-hif1α mice were prepared for subsequent experiments. And AAV-lung-CMV-DIO-EGFP-tWPA-injected CDH5-Cre mice were used as the control group in subsequent experiments.
The LyzM-Cre mice were obtained from Jackson Laboratories (004781). The construction of LyzM-CreDIO-Fgf13 mice and LyzM-CreDIO-hif1α mice followed the same methodology as described above, with the only difference being that CDH5-Cre mice were replaced with LyzM-Cre mice. And AAV-lung-CMV-DIO-EGFP-tWPA-injected LyzM-Cre mice were used as the control group in subsequent experiments.
And we crossed Fgf13 flox/flox mice with CDH5-Cre mice or LyzM-Cre mice to generate Fgf13△Endo mice or Fgf13△mye mice. For experimental purposes, CDH5-Cre mice or LyzM-Cre mice were used as the control group in subsequent experiments.
All mice in our study were housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) environment maintained at constant temperature (22 ± 2 °C) and humidity (40-60%) with a 12/12 h dark-light cycle (light on at 7:00 a.m.), with free access to food and water. Prior to sepsis model induction, male mice (6–8 weeks, 18–23 g) were randomized into experimental groups by laboratory personnel not involved in subsequent experimental procedures. Animals were housed in standard polycarbonate cages (n=5 per cage) and acclimated to the facility environment for 1 week before experimentation. Housing conditions and dietary regimens remained consistent with previously described protocols. Following sepsis model establishment and specimen collection, all phenotypic assessments and biochemical parameter analyses were conducted under single-blind conditions, with evaluators unaware of treatment allocation, to minimize potential observer bias.

Monocyte adhesion assay
HPMECs were plated in a 6-well plate and stimulated with LPS for 12 h. After counting, 1 × 10^6 of THP-1 cells were added to HPMECs in each group at 37 °C for 30 min and then washed twice with warm PBS. Images of each well were photographed using a Nikon Eclipse TE2000-S fluorescence microscope. And the immunofluorescence staining of THP-1 cells in the monocyte adhesion assay was performed according to the process in Immunofluorescence staining. The primary antibodies included: F4/80 (Cell Signaling Technology, 30325). And the fluorescent THP-1 cells were photographed using ZEISS LSM 980 with Airyscan2 Confocal microscope (ZEISS, Germany).

Mass spectrometry analysis
HEK293T cells were transfected with Flag-Fgf13 plasmids, and cells were immunoprecipitated with immunoprecipitation by Flag antibody or IgG (CST, 3900) with protein A/G beads (Meck, LSKMAGAG10). Coimmunoprecipitation was carried out in HEK293T cells and visualized with silver staining by using the Beyotime Fast Silver Stain Kit (Beyotime, P0017S). Then, mass spectrometry was used to detect all the proteins connected with Flag-FGF13. The assay was carried out by Shanghai Bioprofile Technology Company Ltd. In brief, the gradient consisted of 5~35% (v/v) acetonitrile in 0.1% (v/v) formic acid at a flow rate of 200 nL/min for 10 min, 35~100% (v/v) acetonitrile in 0.1% (v/v) formic acid at a flow rate of 200 nL/min for 2 min and 100% acetonitrile in 0.1% formic acid at a flow rate of 200 nL/min for 8 min. The eluted peptides were ionized and introduced into a Thermo Fisher LTQ Velos Pro mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) using a Proxeon nanoelectrospray ion source. Survey full-scan MS spectra (from m/z 200~1800) were acquired. A full mass spectrum (m/z 200~1800) was followed by fragmentation of the ten most abundant peaks, using 35 % of the normalized collision energy for obtaining MS/MS spectra. All peptide assignments were verified by manual inspection. The information about the proteins connected with Flag-Fgf13 was summarized in the Supplementary Materials: Proteins connected with Flag-FGF13.

Plasmid construction and transfection
The Flag-Fgf13 plasmids were constructed by OBiO Technology (Shanghai, China), and HA-TAK1, HA-MEK1, HA-MEK2, HA-ERK1, and HA-ERK2 plasmids were constructed by GENEWIZ (America). Transient transfections for plasmids were performed with Lipo 2000 (Invitrogen, 11668-019) and transfected into HEK293T cells. After transfection for 48 h, HEK293T cells were harvested for co-immunoprecipitation.

Quantification of hemorrhages in the lungs
Mouse lung tissues were washed twice with 0.9% saline and then lysed for 2 h in 1 ml of tissue lysis buffer. Then, 200 µl of lysate was transferred to a 96-well plate at room temperature, and the OD value was measured spectrophotometrically at 400 nm, as described previously55.

Quantification of Wet/Dry weight ratio
After harvest, the lungs of mice from each group were excised and the excess blood was removed. The wet weight of the lungs was measured, and then the lungs were dried in an oven at 37.5 °C for 48 h to determine the dry weight.

Quantitative real-time PCR
Before tested by qRT-PCR, total RNA from samples in each group was extracted using TRI reagent (Sigma, T9424). After measuring the total RNA concentration in each sample, the cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg of RNA according to the manufacturer’s instructions of iScript cDNA Synthesis kit (Bio-Rad, 1708890). Then, qRT-PCR was used to amplify cDNA from samples in each group with specific primers. In addition, the information on specific primers was provided in Table S3. Primer sequences for qRT-PCR.

RNA Interference in HPMECs and THP-1 cells
The Si-Scramble or Si-p53 (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-29435) was mixed with Lipofectamine 2000 in Opti-MEM (Gibco, 51985034) and incubated for 20 min at 37 °C. Then, cells were washed with PBS and incubated in culture medium containing the siRNA mixture. After culturing for 6-8 h, the Opti-MEM mixture was discarded and the cells were washed with PBS. Fresh culture medium was added and the cells were cultured for 48 h prior to use in subsequent experiments.

RNA-seq analysis
RNA-sequencing was performed on the Illumina HiSeqTM 2500/4000 by Gene Denovo Biotechnology Co., Ltd (Guangzhou, China). Total RNA was extracted using Trizol reagent kit (Invitrogen, 12183555) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA quality was assessed on an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, Palo Alto, CA, USA) and checked using RNase-free agarose gel electrophoresis. After total RNA was extracted, eukaryotic mRNA was enriched by Oligo (dT) beads. Then the enriched mRNA was fragmented into short fragments using the fragmentation buffer and reverse transcribed into cDNA by using NEBNext Ultra RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (NEB #7530, New England Biolabs, Ipswich, MA, USA). The purified double-stranded cDNA fragments were end-repaired, A base added, and ligated to Illumina sequencing adapters. The ligation reaction was purified with the AMPure XP Beads (1.0×). And the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplified. The resulting cDNA library was sequenced using Illumina Novaseq 6000 by Gene Denovo Biotechnology Co. (Guangzhou, China).

Sepsis model
Based on the Minimum Quality Threshold in Pre-Clinical Sepsis Studies (MQTiPSS) guidelines, CLP was employed to establish murine sepsis models. The specific CLP procedure was conducted according to the methodology described in a previous investigation56, the specific procedure for CLP is as follows: C57BL/6 male mice (8-10 weeks) were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal (i.p.) injection of pentobarbital sodium (50 mg/kg). Sham-operated mice underwent identical procedures, except for the CLP. In the CLP-induced sepsis model, the caecum of mice was ligated 50% and the ligated cecal stump was then perforated by one “through and through” puncture (21-gauge needle). For LPS-induced endotoxemia sepsis, mice were injected intraperitoneally with a single dose of LPS (10 mg/kg) for 12 h. In both models of sepsis, to inhibit the activation of ERK signaling, SCH772984 (10 mg/kg, i.p.) was used to treat mice 1 h after LPS injection or CLP operation. The serum sample and lungs were harvested after 12 h for further experimentation. After collecting the blood sample, the mice underwent perfusion through the left ventricle with 10 ml of 0.9% saline for 2 minutes. After perfusion, the lungs were extracted from the mice. Following this, the lungs were positioned in a 10 cm diameter culture dish filled with 0.9% saline, and images of the lungs’ appearance were taken. And the remaining tissues were fixed or stored at low temperatures as per the experimental needs.

TUNEL staining in HPMECs
Before incubation with the TUNEL reaction mixture, the process of TUNEL staining in HPMECs is consistent with Immunofluorescence staining. The HPMECs were incubated with a TUNEL reaction mixture (1 h, 37 °C) in a humidified atmosphere in the dark. After washing 3 times with PBS, DAPI was used to stain the nucleus. The phenomenon of TUNEL stain in each group was analyzed (Leica TCS SP8 Confocal microscope (Leica, Wentzler, Germany)), and quantified (ImageQuant 5.2 software (Molecular Dynamics, Sunnyvale, CA)).

Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 8.0 software. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). For comparisons between two groups, unpaired Student’s t-tests were employed. Multiple group comparisons with a single variable were analyzed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test to identify specific intergroup differences. For experimental designs with two variable factors, two-way ANOVA was conducted, followed by Tukey’s post hoc test to determine significant differences between specific groups. Survival analyses were performed using the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Statistical significance was established at p < 0.05 for all analyses.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13), also referred to as FGF homologous factor (FHF) 2, is a member of the FGF11 subfamily that is characterized as having sequence similarities to classical FGF receptor (FGFR)-binding FGFs, but functionally do not bind FGFRs. Similar to other FHFs, FGF13 has been considered a non-secreted protein that lacks an amino signal and is prominently expressed in developing and mature neurons of the central and peripheral nervous systems, as well as the heart. The expression of FGF13 is not limited to early embryonic stages and has been shown to persist in adult tissues. As well, FGF13 is known to localize subcellularly, both within the cytoplasm and the nucleus. In this study, the authors found that FGF13 was down-regulated in endothelial cells and macrophages in lungs from septic mice and sepsis patients. They showed that specific knockout of FGF13 in endothelial cells or macrophages reduced acute lung injury and improved survival in mice with LPS-challenged endotoxic shock. On the other hand, targeted overexpression of FGF13 was found to aggravate acute lung injury and worsen survival in mice with LPS-challenged endotoxic shock. Furthermore, they demonstrated that FGF13 appeared to act as a scaffold protein for the TAK1-MEK-ERK signaling axis and thereby facilitated transmission of the signaling pathway upon LPS stimulation, which promoted HIF-1α-induced aerobic glycolysis in endothelial cells and macrophages, leading to their pro-inflammatory activation. While this study includes interesting findings, I have a number of concerns for the authors to consider.
Major comments are summarized below.
1) In the Methods section, the authors describe that “Before collection the sample from healthy volunteers and sepsis patients, the authors provided the human patient consent forms to healthy volunteers and sepsis patients”. It’s really hard to understand that ‘healthy volunteers’ provided their own lung tissues. In that sense, it’s inconceivable that such a study plan was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University. In addition, patient information should be more fully and specifically provided.
2) The authors should mention what was a post-hoc test following ANOVA.
3) In some animal experiments, an n = 3-4 is not a sufficient experimental number. The insufficient number of samples per test group makes it clear that the study is greatly underpowered. Indeed, in animal experiments, we empirically learn that there are great differences between individuals in mice with lethal endotoxic shock.
4) While LPS plays a pivotal role in the pathogenesis of sepsis, it is well known that LPS-challenged murine models do not fully reflect all factors associated with human sepsis. Thus, LPS infusion is unsuitable animal model for sepsis. LPS-challenged mice should be recognized as an endotoxic shock model but not as a septic model. In this study, the authors used mice with CLP-induced sepsis, which should have been centrally placed in this study.
5) It is very hard to understand the reason why the authors used HUVEC for in vitro experiments. This is a very lame approach. In terms of flow in this study, the authors should have used pulmonary vascular endothelial cells. In the first place, HUVEC is not so much sensitive to LPS. I doubt it’s true that HUVEC responded to 1 μg/mL of LPS in this study.
6) Lung histological images, shown in this paper, are somewhat poor. For routine histology, the authors did not probably use inflation-fixed lungs. Lung histological images are structurally disrupted even in controls. Unfortunately, the readers who are so familiar with the lung histology may not bear to see the histological images presented in this paper.
7) The authors conclude that “targeting FGF13 is a potential therapeutic strategy to alleviate septic lung injury”. However, the authors found that FGF13 was down-regulated in endothelial cells and macrophages in lungs from mice with endotoxic shock or CLP-induced sepsis and patients suffering from sepsis. Given the down-regulation of FGF13 under endotoxic shock or sepsis conditions, whether targeting FGF13 is of high clinically therapeutic value is extremely doubtful.
8) Finally, a major language polishing is required. The manuscript has to definitively use more review for grammar and to help with readability.

Response: Thank you for your constructive suggestions. Here are the main reasons why we chose HEK293 cells for our experiments. First, HEK293 cells are widely used as tool cells for plasmid transfection experiments due to their high transfection efficiency, well-developed protein processing systems, and good stability, making them particularly common in protein interaction studies. Second, at the time of our experiments, there was a lack of commercially available FGF13 antibodies proven to meet the standard requirements for immunoprecipitation experiments, which prevented us from conducting protein interaction studies using cells derived from FGF13 knockout transgenic mice or FGF13 overexpressing transgenic mice. Additionally, as primary macrophages, BMDMs actively eliminate exogenous DNA in cells, resulting in very low plasmid transfection efficiency, making it difficult to achieve the level of target gene overexpression possible with viral vector systems or plasmid transfection in HEK293 cells. Therefore, based on practical considerations, we chose HEK293 cells for Flag-FGF13 plasmid overexpression experiments to verify its binding with components of the TAK1-MEK-ERK axis.
Furthermore, transfecting plasmids in HEK293 cells, combined with co-immunoprecipitation and LC-MS techniques to screen for potential protein interactions, followed by returning to HEK293 cells for plasmid co-transfection and pull-down experiments to verify protein interactions, is currently a highly recognized research approach widely applied in numerous high-quality publications (PMID: 37777507, 36896602, 40202104, 39950300). Additionally, all the plasmids we used contained tag proteins: Flag-FGF13 with a Flag tag, and HA-TAK1, HA-MEK1, HA-MEK2, HA-ERK1, and HA-ERK2 with HA tags. Therefore, in our plasmid overexpression co-immunoprecipitation experiments, we used antibodies against their respective tag proteins (Flag and HA) rather than antibodies against FGF13, TAK1, MEK1, MEK2, ERK1, or ERK2 themselves.This method effectively improved the specificity of immunoprecipitation experiments, significantly reduced background signals and non-specific binding, while also avoiding the potential influence of endogenous FGF13 in HEK293 cells. This method has also been used in the aforementioned high-quality publications to validate protein interactions. We hope you can understand the practical difficulties we encountered. 12. How selective is SCH772984? What are the off-target effects? What is the clinical utility of SCH772984?
Response: Thank you for your question. Below is a point-by-point response to your inquiries.
SCH772984 is a highly selective ERK1/2 inhibitor with a unique binding mechanism. Structural studies revealed that SCH772984 induces the formation of a previously unknown binding pocket between the αC helix and P-loop in ERK1/2 (PMID: 25195011). Its selectivity stems from this distinctive binding mode, which involves three key interactions: indazole binding to the hinge region, pyrrolidine linker interactions with the conserved active site, and phenyl-pyrimidine positioning in the induced P-loop pocket. This creates a highly specific binding profile that distinguishes it from other kinase inhibitors. And the slow dissociation kinetics (25-80 minute half-life) also contributes to its sustained activity. These properties confer high selectivity and low nanomolar inhibition (8.3 nM and 2.7 nM for ERK1 (IC50) and ERK2 (IC50), respectively) of SCH772984 for ERK1/2.
Regarding SCH772984's off-target effects, this study (PMID: 25195011) demonstrates that its inhibitory potency against alternative kinases-including CLK2, DRAK1, and TTK-is dramatically reduced, displaying merely 1/70th to 1/40th of the potency observed against its primary ERK1/2 targets. This pronounced differential in binding affinity highlights the compound's exceptional selectivity profile. Furthermore, structural analyses reveal that SCH772984 adopts canonical yet distinct Type I binding modes when interacting with off-target kinases such as haspin (IC50=398 nM) and JNK1 (IC50=1080 nM), which differs from its unique binding mechanism with ERK1/2.
SCH772984 demonstrates robust inhibition of the ERK signaling pathway, exhibiting remarkable efficacy in suppressing the proliferation of tumor cells resistant to BRAF and MEK inhibitors in preclinical studies (PMID: 23614898, 28143781). Beyond its promising antineoplastic properties, this compound has also shown therapeutic potential in mitigating hepatic ischemia-reperfusion injury (PMID: 38638379). Despite these encouraging findings, SCH772984 has yet to advance to clinical trials due to significant pharmaceutical limitations-specifically its high clearance rate and poor membrane permeability—resulting in sub-optimal absorption and diminished bioavailability in rodent models (PMID: 30934534). To address these pharmaceutical shortcomings, researchers developed MK-8353, an optimized derivative that maintains the therapeutic efficacy while substantially improving drug delivery characteristics. MK-8353 exhibits enhanced oral bioavailability across various species, achieves potent inhibition with IC50 values in the low nanomolar range, and importantly, avoids cross-inhibition of MEK1/2. The phase I clinical trial (MK-8353-001, NCT01358331) evaluated this compound's safety profile, dosing parameters, and preliminary efficacy in 26 patients with metastatic melanoma, colorectal cancer, and other solid tumors. Results indicated that MK-8353 was well-tolerated at doses up to 400 mg twice daily, with measurable anti-tumor responses observed in three of the fifteen evaluable patients—all of whom harbored BRAFV600-mutant melanomas (PMID: 29467321).

Response: We appreciate your thoughtful questions, which raise several points of significant scientific importance. Please find our detailed responses below.
The regulatory role of ERK signaling in HIF-1α is well-established in the literature (PMID: 28928465, 33638620, 37500654, 26579469), thus we did not elaborate extensively on how FGF13 influences this particular mechanism. Nevertheless, to address your specific concerns, we conducted additional experiments to examine this relationship. As is widely recognized in the field, PHD2 (Prolyl Hydroxylase Domain 2) catalyzes the hydroxylation of specific proline residues in HIF-1α, which subsequently targets this transcription factor for degradation via the canonical ubiquitin-proteasome pathway (PMID: 32853548). Previous research has demonstrated that ERK signaling can phosphorylate PHD2 at its Ser125 residue, thereby inhibiting its enzymatic activity. This inhibition consequently reduces HIF-1α hydroxylation, ultimately resulting in HIF-1α protein accumulation (PMID: 31285371). Our investigations yielded results consistent with this established mechanism. Notably, knockdown of Fgf13 produced effects comparable to those observed with attenuated ERK signaling. Specifically, in both HPMECs and THP-1 cell lines, knockdown of Fgf13 significantly diminished the phosphorylation of PHD2 at Ser125, while concurrently enhancing HIF-1α hydroxylation (Fig. R2(A, B)). Furthermore, we observed a marked increase in K48-linked polyubiquitination of HIF-1α following Fgf13 knockdown, providing compelling evidence for accelerated HIF-1α proteasomal degradation under these conditions (Fig. R2(C, D)).
At the same time, there might be a small misunderstanding here. In fact, we did not propose the concept that "FGF13's promotion of ERK signaling occurs on the cytoskeleton." We only demonstrated that FGF13 is a scaffold protein for the TAK1-MEK-ERK signaling axis. Scaffold proteins within cells are not exclusively localized to the cytoskeleton; some scaffold proteins (KSR, caveolin, et al.) are predominantly found in the cytoplasm and on the cell membrane (PMID: 11309192, 11741534, 9045678, 22142403). Previous studies have shown that FGF13 binds to microtubules and can stabilize them (PMID: 22726441, 34533854); therefore, we believe the concept that "FGF13's promotion of ERK signaling occurs on the cytoskeleton" may also be reasonable.
To further validate our hypothesis regarding the expression-dependent function of FGF13, we extended our studies to include A549 cells as an additional experimental model. This choice was informed by two key considerations: first, A549 cells, consistent with many cancer cell lines, exhibit relatively high endogenous FGF13 expression levels that significantly exceed those observed in BEAS-2B cells (Fig. R5A); second, as A549 cells are characterized by constitutively elevated ERK signaling typical of cancer cells, we deemed LPS stimulation unnecessary for ERK activation in this context (PMID: 34533854, 31256425). Our metabolic analyses employing 2-NBDG fluorescence and glucose uptake/lactate secretion assays demonstrated that knockdown of Fgf13 significantly attenuated both glucose consumption and lactate production in A549 cells. Conversely, overexpression of Fgf13 further augmented these glycolytic parameters, an effect that was abolished by co-treatment with SCH772984 (Fig. R5(B-E)).
Collectively, these findings support our conclusion that the cell-type selectivity of FGF13's effects on aerobic glycolysis primarily reflects its differential expression patterns across cell types. In cells where FGF13 is abundantly expressed (endothelial cells, macrophages, and certain cancer cells), it serves as a critical regulator of glycolytic metabolism. Moreover, our gain-of-function experiments indicate that when expressed at sufficient levels in other cell types, such as epithelial cells, FGF13 is competent to enhance aerobic glycolysis through ERK-dependent mechanisms.
Addressing the question of whether FGF13's enhancement of aerobic glycolysis is LPS-specific or extends across diverse cellular stimuli, we present here relevant findings from our recent unpublished investigations. The scientific literature has firmly established that both hyperglycemic conditions and OX-LDL exposure can induce aerobic glycolysis in macrophages, thereby promoting their pro-inflammatory phenotype (PMID: 33044562, 36878047). In our experimental paradigm utilizing THP-1 cells, we observed that knockdown of Fgf13 significantly attenuated multiple parameters of glycolytic metabolism under high glucose conditions, including overall glycolytic capacity, glucose uptake, and lactate production. Interestingly, this dependency on FGF13 exhibited stimulus specificity, as knockdown of Fgf13 failed to modulate aerobic glycolysis in THP-1 cells exposed to OX-LDL (Fig. R6(A-C)). These differential responses provide compelling evidence that FGF13's metabolic regulatory function is stimulus-dependent rather than universally applicable across all pro-inflammatory activators. Further mechanistic investigation revealed that the ERK inhibitor SCH772984 effectively suppressed the enhanced glycolytic phenotype induced by Fgf13 overexpression in high glucose-stimulated THP-1 cells-a pattern identical to our observations in LPS-stimulated conditions (Fig. R6(D-F)). This pharmacological evidence suggests a conserved molecular mechanism underlying FGF13's promotion of aerobic glycolysis in both LPS and high glucose contexts, likely operating through the ERK signaling pathway.
Regarding the differential expression pattern of FGF13 across cell types, it is important to clarify that FGF13 is not absent in non-endothelial or non-macrophage cells, but rather exhibits substantially lower expression levels in these other cell populations. In addition to the pronounced expression observed in endothelial cells and macrophages, FGF13 has been documented to be expressed in neurons and cardiomyocytes, suggesting tissue-specific regulatory mechanisms (PMID: 28162808, 23804213). Despite our extensive experimental investigations, the molecular determinants governing this cell type-specific expression profile of FGF13 remain elusive. To our knowledge, no comprehensive studies have systematically addressed the underlying mechanisms responsible for this selective expression pattern. We postulate that this phenomenon may be attributed to several potential regulatory mechanisms: 1.Transcriptional regulation: The transcription factors responsible for activating FGF13 gene expression may themselves display cell type-specific distribution patterns, thereby restricting robust FGF13 expression to particular cellular lineages. 2.Epigenetic regulation: The Fgf13 locus may be subject to differential epigenetic modifications across cell types, including DNA methylation patterns, histone modifications, and chromatin accessibility states that collectively determine transcriptional permissiveness.
We anticipate that employing multidisciplinary approaches will be instrumental in elucidating these regulatory mechanisms. Specifically, techniques such as single-cell lineage tracing, comprehensive transcriptomic profiling, proteomic analysis of chromatin-associated complexes, and genome-wide epigenetic mapping will likely provide valuable insights into the determinants of FGF13's cell type-specific expression. These methodologies, particularly when applied in an integrated fashion, hold considerable promise for resolving this fundamental question in future investigations.

I thank the authors for their extensive and careful responses to both sets of reviewer comments, and for undertaking substantial revisions and additional experiments. The manuscript is clearly improved in clarity, methodological transparency, and scope. Below I provide my assessment of how the major issues have been addressed.
1. Methods, Transparency, and Ethics
The incorporation of methodological details from the supplemental materials into the main text significantly improves readability. The corrected and clarified ethics statement, together with inclusion of approval and consent documents, addresses concerns from both reviewers.
2. Models of Sepsis and Experimental Design
The addition of the CLP model is a major improvement that strengthens the translational relevance of the work and addresses the limitation of relying solely on LPS. Revisions regarding randomization, blinding, housing, and ARRIVE/MQTiPSS guidelines improve rigor and reporting.
3. Statistical Analyses
The re-analysis of data using appropriate statistical approaches is appreciated. I encourage the authors to ensure that figure legends clearly specify the statistical tests, post-hoc corrections, and sample sizes, as this was a central concern from both reviewers. The issue of relatively small n (3–4 in some experiments) is partly mitigated by transparency but remains a limitation that should be explicitly acknowledged.
4. Cell Models
Replacing HUVECs with HPMECs is an important correction. The justification for using HEK293 cells for protein–protein interaction studies is well explained, though it remains a limitation in terms of physiological relevance and should be discussed explicitly.
5. Histology
Reviewer #2’s concerns about poor lung histology images were significant. The authors state that new, higher-quality images have been provided. If the revised figures indeed meet standard quality, this point is resolved; otherwise, histology remains a weakness.
6. Specificity of FGF13 Regulation
The additional data in myocardial infarction and previous findings in diabetic nephropathy suggest that downregulation of FGF13 is not specific to sepsis, but may reflect a broader injury/stress signature. This is an important contextualization and should be framed in the discussion to avoid overstating specificity.
7. Mechanism and Scope
The additional experiments on ERK/HIF1α signaling, glycolysis, and cell-type specificity strengthen the mechanistic claims. The evidence that effects are stimulus- and expression-dependent is convincing. However, conclusions should be moderated to emphasize context dependence rather than universal application.
8. Therapeutic Implications
The paradox that FGF13 is downregulated in sepsis yet contributes to injury is intriguing. The authors provide thoughtful mechanistic explanations (p53 regulation, enhanced protein interactions despite downregulation). Nevertheless, therapeutic claims should be tempered, given these complexities and the translational uncertainties.
9. Presentation and Language
The manuscript has been substantially revised for clarity and language. The addition of a limitations section and corrections to references are appreciated.
Minor Comments –
Clarifications - in page 5 line 105 please re-word or clarify LPS is a model sterile injury.
Language – there are still minor problems with editing language: e.g., Line 118 “FGFs critically regulate lung development…” the phrasing does not make much sense: Do you mean FGF is a critical regulator of lung development OR FGF’s critical regulation during lung development? Removing redundancies would also help reading e.g. in both no-sepsis patients and sepsis patients – this could be changed to both non-septic and septic patients. Again – employing a language editor to go through the manuscript would significantly improve understanding by the reader.
Overall Assessment
This manuscript has undergone extensive revision and addresses many of the key methodological and interpretive issues raised in the first round of review. Remaining limitations include the breadth of claims regarding specificity, the paradox of downregulation versus pathogenicity, and the reliance on certain cell models.
